title: Neutrino hunters: Searching for ghostly particles in Antarctic ice, with Abby Vieregg
excerpt: Astrophysicist leads launch of NASA balloon to detect high-energy particles from the cosmos
content:
Paul Rand: Right now, there are trillions of tiny particles passing through our bodies, leaving no trace and causing no harm. They’re called neutrinos, commonly known as “ghost particles.”

Abby Vieregg: Neutrinos are fundamental particles, which means they can't be broken down into smaller pieces. They're tiny. They can travel through light years of space without interacting with the dust and light that's in space. They can come all the way from the Big Bang, travel 13.8 billion years without ever interacting. 

Paul Rand: That’s Abby Vieregg, professor of physics and astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Chicago. Vieregg has devoted her career to trying to hunt down neutrinos.

Abby Vieregg: If it was easy, it would have been done by now. It's like a paradox. The thing that makes neutrinos a beautiful messenger particle to learn about very distant things in the universe and to learn the things inside energetic engines in the universe. The same property that makes them perfect for that, makes them really hard to detect.

Paul Rand: Vieregg and her team have spent years building detectors to beat the odds and find these neutrinos.

Abby Vieregg: So how do you build a detector to do this? So the answer, unfortunately, is you really need a really big detector and even still, even though those detectors are really big, you still don't see most of the neutrinos that go through. Most of them go right through and never hit anything.

Paul Rand: They needed something big, and it also needed to be radio transparent, so that radio waves could pass through it without being blocked or absorbed.

Abby: It turns out that glacial ice is quite radio transparent. So we built a NASA balloon mission called PUEO, the Payload for Ultra High Energy Observations. And the balloon flies 40 kilometers above the Antarctic ice sheet. And what we do is we look down at the Antarctic ice sheet for neutrino interactions in the ice. And we're basically using the entire Antarctic continent as our detector.

Paul Rand: So the question remains: Will they be able to do it?

Paul Rand: From the University of Chicago Podcast Network, welcome to Big Brains, where we explore the groundbreaking research and the ideas that are changing our world. I’m your host, Paul Rand. Join me as we meet the minds behind the breakthroughs. On today’s episode, the hunt for neutrinos, the “ghost“ particle, and experiments taking place in some of the world’s most extreme environments.

Paul Rand: If you appreciate hearing from experts in research and science that are shaping our world, please consider subscribing to the Big Brains YouTube channel. It ensures that you never miss an episode and it helps these important conversations reach a broader audience of learners.

Paul Rand: And finally, on a personal note: It is bittersweet to share that after almost nine years, this is my final episode of Big Brains. It has been a true pleasure and an honor to share these stories with you. Thank you for joining me. An incredible team is behind Big Brains, and my longtime colleague Jeremy Manier will take over as host. There are many more Big Brains to come.

What are neutrinos?

Paul Rand: One of the things I just wanted to establish an understanding out of the gate: Even while we're sitting here, there are trillions of particles that are flowing through your body and mind, but neither of us feels them in any which way. And if I have this right: That's kind of what you've spent a career chasing. What are those particles and how do we think about them?

Abby Vieregg: It is true. There are trillions of particles passing through our body all the time, and those particles are called neutrinos. And I like to think about neutrinos as they're kind of like the sister particle to a particle that we know and love called the electron.

Why are neutrinos called ghost particles?

Paul Rand: The other term I've heard used to describe them as ghost particles. Is that a fair name?

Abby Vieregg: The reason why people call them ghost particles is because they have no charge, they don't interact with charged particles in the normal way. And so neutrinos are weekly interacting. That's the only sort of fundamental interaction they can have. And that means that they can travel through our bodies without interacting. They can travel through light years of space without interacting with the dust and light that's in space. They can come all the way from the Big Bang, travel 13.8 billion years without ever interacting.

Abby Vieregg: So I have started off by talking about the most abundant neutrinos, which is from the Big Bang. But actually the neutrinos I spend a lot of time thinking about are neutrinos that come from very dense energetic engines in the universe, like the most big black holes that suck in particles, suck in dust, and then that's called accreting. They accrete dust and then they spit out jets of particles. So those jets of particles include lots of neutrinos. But one thing that's kind of interesting is that for certain kinds of sources like that, it's sitting in a bath of dust. There's stuff around it. And so the regular light that gets emitted gets absorbed by that dust, but the neutrinos can come right to us. And what we can do is get a map of what the central engine looks like.

Paul Rand: But if they go through everything in the way that you're talking about, how do you even detect one?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, that's the question. If it was easy, it would've been done by now. It's like a paradox. The thing that makes neutrinos a beautiful messenger particle to learn about very distant things in the universe and to learn about the things inside energetic engines in the universe, the same property that makes them perfect for that makes them really hard to detect because you can imagine the flip side is, all right, it passes through our bodies. Most neutrinos pass through the whole earth without interacting. So how do you build a detector to do this?

Abby Vieregg: So the answer, unfortunately, is you really need a really big detector. So pretty much all neutrino detectors are really big. And even still, even though those detectors are really big, you still don't see most of the neutrinos that go through. Most of them go right through and never hit anything. But once in a while, one of the neutrinos hits something in your detector and knocks a nucleus out basically, and then that makes a little particle shower that makes light and you can go look for that. So that's how most neutrino detectors work, is like imagine a big block or vat of stuff, big meaning... I mean, we can talk about how big big is. Big meaning either something that you could maybe build at a place on a national lab scale at a place like Fermilab, or big meaning even bigger, you can't even build a building big enough to fit it inside.

Paul Rand: Can you help me understand that a little bit better, please?

Why is it so difficult to detect neutrinos?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah. One of the ways to look for high-energy neutrinos is you build a big detector, right?

Paul Rand: OK.

Abby Vieregg: A neutrino hits an atom in your material. It knocks that atom out and the nucleus of that atom quickly makes a particle shower. That particles in that shower are actually moving faster than the speed of light in the material that you're in, which is a little confusing because probably someone somewhere along the way said things can't move faster than the speed of light. And that's true, but that's for the speed of light in vacuum. So in a material, the speed of light is slower and you can actually get particles that move faster than the speed of light in that material. It's kind of like a sonic boom. So an airplane goes faster than the speed of sound, you get a sonic boom. A particle moves faster than the speed of light in a material and you get the light equivalent of that. That's called Cherenkov radiation.

Abby Vieregg: And it turns out the Askaryan effect, it turns out is that at very long wavelength... So you'll very quickly learn that I love neutrinos and I love cosmology, but I'm really a radio nerd. That's really what I spend most of my time thinking about is radio waves. And the reason is because particles, when you make a particle shower in a material like that and you get this Cherenkov emission, that's the sonic boom that you get, but in light, if you look at the part of the spectrum of light that's in radio waves... So radio waves have very long wavelengths compared to optical light and compared to the size of these showers. So if you look at something that has very long wavelength compared to the size of the shower, then what you end up with is that all the light from that shower is emitted coherently.

Abby Vieregg: And coherence is one of my favorite tricks in physics. We have 10 billion electrons in our particle shower made by this one neutrino, ultimately. Those 10 billion electrons all emit radiation at the same time. And for long wavelengths, it gives this big boost in the amount of power that you see when all of those wiggling electrons look to the outside observer like they're emitting at the same time for those wavelengths. So that's what coherence is. It's when a bunch of things move together in the same way. And often what it does is it sort of boosts the signal that you see.

Paul Rand: You have found that ice can become part of a particle detector. And I wonder if you can explain that and why ice instead of water or rock or any other type of material?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah. OK. So to look for the highest energy neutrinos, we're going to look for this coherent radio emission. That called a Askaryan emission. So what we need is a really big detector made of a radio transparent material. So you need something that the radio waves that are made will travel through the material so then you can build an antenna to detect them basically.

Paul Rand: OK. All right.

Abby Vieregg: And then you need it to be relatively dense. So if you tried to build a detector out of gas, it wouldn't work that well. So you need something relatively dense so you have a higher chance of interaction. It turns out that glacial ice is quite radio transparent.

Paul Rand: So it's a relatively new experience as you're talking about it. And you were in the news quite a bit in the last year because you put five years of your work into this area under a NASA balloon and kind of let it fly away over Antarctica.

Abby Vieregg: Yeah.

Paul Rand: Take me back to that morning, what you had been working to and what you were trying to do with the experiment that you entrusted all your work to.

What is the NASA mission called PUEO?

Abby Vieregg: So we built a NASA balloon mission called PUEO, the payload for ultra-high energy observations. It's a detector that's designed to look for the highest energy astrophysical neutrinos. And the reason why it's on a balloon, it's basically a bunch of antennas strapped to a balloon and the balloon flies 40 kilometers above the Antarctic ice sheet. And what we do is we look down at the Antarctic ice sheet for neutrino interactions in the ice.

Paul Rand: 20-ish miles up or so?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, about 20 miles up, 120,000 feet. And we're basically using the entire Antarctic continent as our detector. That's why we're on a balloon. We're on a balloon so we can see everywhere all at once. It's a little bit of a kind of crazy experiment, I have to say, but it's really fun. And as far as I know, it's the only way to do that. And every day we would wake up in basically dorm rooms in McMurdo Station in Antarctica, which is the main US base actually run by the National Science Foundation. So NASA and NSF worked together to make this happen. We'd wake up in our dorms, we'd go to the galley to have breakfast in the morning, and then we'd catch a bus out to the balloon facility, which is about a 30-minute drive away. And then the balloon facility has the hangars where we do our work for the scientific payloads. There were two payloads this last year, which is a normal number.

Paul Rand: My understanding is you took out about 50 to 60 terabytes of data, but you're not getting the answer on the spot. It's going to take almost a year or so to do it.

Abby Vieregg: Yes.

Paul Rand: Is that tough to wait all that time and through all this work when you just want to unwrap it?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah. I feel like one of the things, it's fun to look at it through my eyes and also look at it through my students' eyes. So I actually was a grad student on one of the previous balloon missions, sort of predecessor to this project. So I really can relate to my grad students these days on this particular project and the kind of agony they're feeling of wanting to get to the end and find out the answer. But we got our hard drives. We launched in December. We got the mission terminated in January, we got 23 days, which is about what we expected. So we got our team of 16 people...

Paul Rand: Wow, OK.

Abby Vieregg: Got down to Antarctica in early November, and then we declared flight readiness in sort of mid-December. So it took us four or five weeks to really get ready. It takes a bit of work and check everything and make sure it's working because you only get one shot. It has to work the first time. And we declared flight readiness. And then actually, unfortunately, I had to go home. So after we declared flight readiness, I went home.

Paul Rand: Was that disappointing?

Abby Vieregg: Oh man, it was so disappointing. It was very disappointing because we were very close to launching and I thought I was going to be there for launch. And then about a-third of our team had to go home basically because there's a long flight gap over the holidays.

Paul Rand: Got it.

Abby Vieregg: And if you stay, then you're stuck for six weeks.

Paul Rand: Oh gosh, OK.

Abby Vieregg: And essentially those of us with children had to go home.

Paul Rand: Understood.

Abby Vieregg: Because you can't just sit around if... Yeah, you can't stay in Antarctica that long. So I stayed to declare flight readiness, and then it was actually... So I got on the flight from Antarctica with a few other... Yeah, sorry, from Antarctica back to New Zealand with a few other people, and we launched the next morning. So I actually watched it from the hotel room in Christchurch, New Zealand with everyone else who was in Christchurch at the time who had just come off the ice. And yeah, it was hard. It was hard and we were disappointed that we couldn't be there for sure. But I will say that my grad students and postdocs ran the show and they did the hard work.

Abby Vieregg: Launching this thing is stressful. I mean, the guys from NASA actually launch it, but making sure our instrument passes the final checks and is actually functioning and that you're giving the thumbs up to go.

Paul Rand: Really amazing. Now we're coming up on a few months away from a year. Have you caught anything or noticed anything or learned anything yet or does it all kind of just come to light at the magical year mark?

Abby Vieregg: It all comes to light at the end, unfortunately. Well, unfortunately, it comes to light at the end, and that's on purpose actually. So the way we do the analysis, this is the way nearly all analyses in particle physics are done, we usually do it blind. So if you're searching for something new that no one has seen before... And no one has seen neutrinos at these energies before, this would be the highest energy neutrino anybody's ever seen if we're successful. When you're searching for something new and you expect to only find a few of the things... We might see a few events from different sources, and that would be a big deal if we did because no one has seen them before. When you're looking for just a few things in a sea of backgrounds, you're looking for kind of the needle in a haystack.

Paul Rand: Literally.

Abby Vieregg: Yeah. You don't want to do it just by flipping through to see if the next thing looks like the needle you're looking for. You want to do it in a systematic way that allows you to characterize all of the backgrounds you're seeing and then really understand your data set. And then at the end you ask, "Hey, did we see any neutrinos?"

Where do high-energy neutrinos come from?

Paul Rand: You're now talking about these ultra-high energy neutrinos, and can you help us understand what makes them different and where in the universe they were made and how they were made?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah. So ultra-high energy neutrinos come from, as might not surprise you, the most energetic places in the universe. We actually don't know... I would say one of the main reasons we built this experiment is that we don't know where the highest energy particles in the universe come from actually. So people have made measurements of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, which are charged particles like protons or iron nuclei coming from places in the universe. But the problem with charged particles is that charged particles bend in magnetic fields, so they don't travel in a straight path. And we live in a galaxy that has a magnetic field. So anything that comes from outside our galaxy to us gets scrambled up in the magnetic field of our galaxy if it's a charged particle. So you can detect ultra-high energy cosmic rays, which people have done, namely the Auger experiment, which one of the main leaders of the Auger experiment was Jim Cronin, who was on the faculty here for a very long time and won a Nobel Prize.

Abby Vieregg: So measuring ultra-high energy cosmic rays is something that has been done, but figuring out where they come from, what is the set of sources that makes those particles, you can't really do it with charged particles because they're all scrambled. And so if instead we can look for their neutrino counterparts, the neutrinos are not charged, so they come straight from the sources.

Paul Rand: OK. Can you explain to me though what you could potentially see if you found one of these ultra-high energy?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah. We basically are trying to learn what the physics that drives the central engines of the most energetic places in the universe is. So what are the magnetic fields like in those sources? How big are those sources? What are the sort of physical interactions that are happening in those sources so that we can learn how they work? And we don't quite know which sources it is, but we have a good guess because of other things we've looked at like cosmic rays and gamma rays, which are sort of high energy light, that it could be this active galactic nucleus category of sources that I talked about earlier, big black holes are creating matter and spitting out jets of particles. It could be the highest energy particles could come from things like binary neutron star mergers, which is what also make gravitational waves that LIGO has seen. They could come from pulsars, which can also produce high-energy particles.

Abby Vieregg: So I think there's a few hypotheses and we'd like to figure out which or what sum, what total of sources is making the high energy particle flux so that we can learn about the physics inside of them.

What is the ANITA experiment?

Paul Rand: Tell me about ANITA.

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, so ANITA was kind of the predecessor to PUEO. ANITA was the balloon experiment that I actually worked on as a grad student, and ANITA had four flights actually from Antarctica, so it took quite a bit of data. And really the advancement for PUEO, why did we decide many years later to fly it again and do it again, is we figured out how to make the detector at least a factor of 10 more sensitive than the ANITA flights. And I figured that once we figured out how to make a much more sensitive detector by building basically more sensitive electronics, then we should fly it again. So ANITA really was the sort of predecessor to PUEO, and then we had a technology jump that allowed us to do PUEO.

Paul Rand: So if I remember this right, it picked up two radio pulses that came out of the ice that, for lack of a better way of phrasing it, shouldn't have been there.

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, that's right.

Paul Rand: What was so strange about them?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, so ANITA, again, was built to look for this Askaryan emission, the coherent radio emission from neutrino interactions in the ice. But it turns out that ANITA and PUEO are actually also sensitive to a very different kind of signal that usually comes from cosmic rays actually. And that signal is when a cosmic ray makes a particle shower in the atmosphere, actually not in the ice, but in the atmosphere. And because we're on a balloon, we're above almost all the atmosphere. So when we look down at the ice, we look essentially through the atmosphere to see the signals from the ice. And so sometimes we actually see signals from cosmic rays, which have been seen at these energies that make air showers. They make showers in the atmosphere, and we see radio emission from that. That is known and understood, and we see tens of those per flight on ANITA.

Abby Vieregg: All of those radio signals should look about the same because it's the same physics and it's the same geometry essentially. But on actually two of the flights of ANITA, there was kind of one event per flight that looked a heck of a lot like a cosmic ray air shower, kind of a boring vanilla cosmic ray air shower, except the signal was flipped in our time streams in the... The signal, the electric field that we measure with our detector was flipped with respect to the other events. So we saw, let's say, 20 events that all look the same, and then we see one event that looks the same, but exactly inverted. Then you're like, "Okay, well, how do you get something that looks inverted?"

Abby Vieregg: One way to get something that looks inverted is by reflecting it off of something. Okay, so it turns out that the cosmic rays we see, it's a little bit of a confusing story, the cosmic rays we see, the way we see them is a cosmic ray, the radio waves actually reflect off the ice and come back to ANITA. So every cosmic ray we see has been reflected.

Abby Vieregg: And so the one weird event is an event that looks like an event that has not been reflected because it's the opposite direction. So you ask what could make a radio pulse that looks a lot like an air shower that has not been reflected off the ice? And one answer is you have a neutrino that comes... As I said earlier, neutrinos usually pass right through the earth. So you could have a neutrino that passes right through most of the earth and then decays... Well, it would have to interact somewhere in the earth, and then the particles that are made in that interaction decay when they come out of the earth and make essentially an air shower, but with opposite sign from the cosmic rays.

Abby Vieregg: So those are the two events that ANITA saw. They look a lot like the cosmic ray events in every way, but with opposite, we call it polarity, opposite polarity where the signal looks inverted. And one explanation is a neutrino that came through the earth and made up air shower. There's some weirdness about that though, I will say, and that's because the two events, they don't quite fit all the profile you would expect for an upward going neutrino like that. They're too steeply upgoing, so they come too steep up to the detector. If we saw a few like that, we should have expected to see many more out to the horizon, and we didn't see that. So we call them internally, we call them mystery events when we are sitting on telecoms and we're like, "Oh, but the mystery events." I think that's just... We don't know what they are.

Paul Rand: What I remember is that the internet figured it out for you.

Abby Vieregg: Yes, the internet did figure it out for us. That's right.

Evidence of a parallel universe?

Paul Rand: So there's some brilliance there. And if I remember it right, they thought about this as this was evidence of a parallel universe?

Abby Vieregg: Right. Yeah. The internet figured that out for us. Yes.

Paul Rand: That's amazing. Was that hard to look at some of these assumptions coming out of your data?

Abby Vieregg: Oh, you know what? I feel like a lot of times our... I often feel like my job as an experimentalist is to build the best experiment I can, analyze the data, and present the results that we have to the community. And at that point, you do what you can, you present the results to the community, and we never say, "This is a detection of dark matter." Some people thought it was parallel universe, dark matter, neutrinos, beyond standard model, whatever, various things came out of that. And I think that's actually kind of healthy not for the internet to come up with the answer, but I think it's kind of healthy for the field to have people who think about questions we want to go answer, build an experiment, and then present the results. And then we have a separate group of people who are theorists who then look at that data and say, "Ah, what else could it be?"

Paul Rand: Got it.

Abby Vieregg: And then you get some papers from people who thought about, "Oh, could this be some other thing?" I actually think that's quite healthy. And some of them are a bit more preposterous than others, but-

Paul Rand: You don't know.

Abby Vieregg: We don't know. And honestly, that's kind of a matter of taste. I don't want to have my own predetermined biases that the standard model is correct, determine, I don't know, what I think things could be.

What is the RNO-G experiment?

Paul Rand: So the other one, and I think you're doing this now, is you're building another array called RNO-G in Greenland.

Abby Vieregg: Yes.

Paul Rand: What are you hoping to learn from that experiment?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, so the Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland, RNO-G. Oh, it's a very similar idea to PUEO. We have a bunch of radio antennas that are looking for radio signals from neutrinos. The difference is rather than flying them on a balloon and looking at 700 kilometers in every direction of Antarctica all at once, we put sets of antennas spaced a few kilometers apart from each other near the surface of the ice, and then we make an array of antennas like that. And the reason you actually want to do both experiments. One, PUEO sees lots of ice, but is kind of far away from the ice. And so far away means that the signals have to be really bright when they're made for you to see them. And what that translates to is they have to be very high energy. So they have to be bright, the neutrinos have to be very high energy.

Abby Vieregg: If you want to build a detector that looks for a little bit lower energy neutrinos, still sort of in the range that KM3NeT has now seen, but maybe a little bit higher as well, then you have to get your detector closer to the ice. And so that's what RNO-G is. It's a set of radio antennas that we're building at a place called Summit Station in Greenland, which is a National Science Foundation run base in the center of Greenland, and it's complimentary to PUEO in that way.

Paul Rand: Now that we've got the basic understanding of neutrinos and what's going on, when we see news stories coming up or we learn about advancements, what should we be keeping an eye out for?

Abby Vieregg: Yeah, I mean, I think the interesting things in neutrino astrophysics, I break into two different categories. I've talked a lot about the astrophysics, so can we learn where these neutrinos are coming from? So I think to me, if I look forward in the next 10 years, like what are the most interesting things going to be, it's going to be experiments like Ice Cube and these radio experiments we're building working together with other data sets to try to identify the sources of them, of neutrinos and characterize them. So if you were to see articles in science news or scientific articles out there, I think in the next 10 years, the thing that in neutrino astrophysics that'll be interesting is to see if we can make measurements of the highest energies that no one has made before and figure out where these things are coming from. So I think that'll happen one way or another. I also think that there's a particle physics aspect to this that's less likely to hit the news headlines in the next 10 years, in my opinion, but if it does, would be more interesting.

Paul Rand: And what's that?

Abby Vieregg: And that's that by measuring neutrinos at energies that we cannot make here on earth, you can't build an accelerator big enough here on earth to make these things, it's possible that we could learn something about particle physics itself from measuring these neutrinos. Either we could learn something about the properties of neutrinos themselves, maybe we'll learn that they decay, which would be a big thing in particle physics. It would shake the sort of underpinnings of how it all works, or maybe we'll learn that... These neutrinos are at energies so high and coming from so far away that there's no other way to probe that set of parameters in physics. So maybe we'll learn something that breaks the standard model, I guess, is a way to put it, which would be really cool. It seems less likely to me, but if it does, then you'll see it on the front page of at least the science section in the New York Times.

Paul Rand: OK.

Paul Rand: Bold and curious. These words describe the guests that you hear on Big Brains who are shaping the future of research.
